name: Tomato
perishability: Highly perishable. Ripe fruit lasts 2–5 days at room temperature.
summary: Grown somewhere in India in every month, but the crop cannot be stored, so supply follows the weather week by week. Prices are lowest in the January–March glut and usually peak in July–August, when monsoon rain and earlier heat damage hit the southern and hill crops at the same time.

key_numbers.label: Production 2024-25
key_numbers.note: Final; down from 213.2 lakh t in 2023-24

key_numbers.label: Post-harvest loss
key_numbers.note: farm 8.37% + market 3.25%; among the highest of all crops

global: India is the second-largest tomato producer after China. Exports are small (mainly Bangladesh, Nepal, UAE, Oman) because the fruit does not travel well.

rows.hubs: Bihar, Telangana, UP, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh (summer), Uttarakhand

belts.name: Kolar–Chikkaballapur
belts.note: Kolar APMC is one of Asia's largest tomato markets; ships to North India, Bangladesh and the Gulf.

belts.name: Madanapalle
belts.note: Huge summer (Apr–Jun) market; supplies Chennai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru.

belts.name: Narayangaon–Junnar
belts.note: Kharif and rabi crops for Mumbai and the North.

belts.name: Solan–Sirmaur
belts.note: Hill crop, Jun–Sep, filling the monsoon gap in North India.

belts.name: Malwa and Nimar
belts.note: Large winter crop feeding North and Central India.

seasons.name: Kharif
seasons.note: Monsoon crop; disease pressure is high.

seasons.name: Rabi / winter
seasons.region: MP, Karnataka, AP, Gujarat, Odisha, WB
seasons.note: Largest crop; causes the Jan–Mar glut.

seasons.name: Summer
seasons.note: Fruit set suffers in heat waves.

seasons.name: Hill (off-season)
seasons.note: Critical for North India in the monsoon.

lean_season: June–August, and again in October–November after heavy late rains.

climate.v: 21–24 °C ideal. Fruit set fails above 32 °C (day) or 21 °C (night), and below 10 °C.
Red pigment (lycopene) forms best at 21–24 °C and stops above 30 °C, so summer fruit turns orange-yellow.
Prefers a dry season with irrigation. Heavy rain causes fruit cracking, blight and rot.
Well-drained loam, pH 6.0–7.0; staked crops on raised beds with drip and mulch are now common.
Killed by frost; winter crops in the North are planted to avoid Dec–Jan cold.

weather_risks.impact: Flower drop and poor fruit set cut the summer crop that should supply July.
weather_risks.example: 2023: April–June heat plus whitefly-borne viruses set up the July spike.

weather_risks.impact: Fruit rot and blight; landslides block hill supply routes.
weather_risks.example: July 2023: Himachal floods cut the Solan supply line.

weather_risks.impact: Damages the kharif harvest in the South.
weather_risks.example: Nov 2021: heavy rains in the South pushed retail to ₹80–100/kg.

weather_risks.impact: Damages winter crop and slows ripening.

pests.name: Tomato leaf curl virus (ToLCV)
pests.impact: Stunting and curled leaves; can wipe out summer crops.

pests.name: Cucumber mosaic virus (CMV)
pests.impact: Large outbreaks in Karnataka and Maharashtra in 2023 contributed to the price spike.

pests.name: South American pinworm
pests.impact: Invasive since 2014; mines leaves and fruit.

pests.name: Fruit borer
pests.impact: Bores into fruit; heavy losses without control.

pests.name: Early blight / late blight
pests.impact: Leaf and fruit blight in humid and rainy weather.

pests.name: Bacterial wilt
pests.impact: Sudden wilting in warm, wet soils.

pests.name: Groundnut bud necrosis virus
pests.impact: Necrotic rings on fruit; common in the South.

postharvest.storage: Mature-green: 12–15 °C, 85–95% RH. Ripe: 8–10 °C for a few days.
postharvest.shelf_ambient: 2–5 days ripe; about a week if picked at the breaker stage.
postharvest.respiration: Climacteric; produces ethylene and ripens after harvest. Keep away from ethylene-sensitive leafy vegetables and cauliflower.
postharvest.chilling: Chilling injury below ~10 °C (mature-green) or ~7 °C (ripe): uneven ripening, pitting, rot.
practices: For long hauls, fruit is picked at the breaker or turning stage so it ripens in transit.
Packed in plastic crates or wooden boxes; Kolar trades in roughly 15 kg crates, many other markets in 25 kg crates.
Less than 1% is processed; India still imports tomato paste.
Gluts end with fruit dumped on roads when the price falls below the cost of picking and freight.

steps.what: Hand-picked every 3–4 days over 2–3 months; sorted by colour stage.
Kolar, Madanapalle, Narayangaon and Pimpalgaon auction crate by crate; a commission agent settles.
Repack and send trucks to Delhi, Kolkata, Bangladesh border and Gulf exporters.
Vendors and quick commerce; retail mark-up is widest when prices are rising.

supply_chain.packaging: Plastic or wooden crates (15–25 kg). Open trucks, rarely refrigerated.

markets.name: Kolar APMC
markets.role: Largest tomato market in South India; sets national tone in Jul–Dec.

varieties.name: Arka Rakshak, Arka Samrat
varieties.note: ICAR-IIHR hybrids with triple disease resistance.

varieties.name: Abhinav, Saho, US-440, NS-585
varieties.note: Popular private hybrids: firm, long shelf life.

varieties.name: Desi (round, soft, sour) vs Hybrid (firm, oval)
varieties.note: Traded and priced separately in most markets.

trade.exports: Small; mostly to Bangladesh, Nepal, UAE, Oman, Qatar.
trade.imports: Negligible fresh; occasional Nepal imports in 2023. India imports tomato paste.

policy.what: NCCF and NAFED bought tomato in Kolar and Madanapalle and sold it at subsidised prices in Delhi-NCR and other cities, starting at ₹90/kg and cutting to ₹50/kg by mid-August.
Operation Greens (MoFPI) covers tomato: freight and storage subsidies during gluts.
No minimum support price. Some states run Market Intervention Schemes in gluts.

history.what: Unseasonal rain in AP, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu; retail ₹80–120/kg.
Heat, viral disease and floods together; retail ₹200–250/kg in several cities.
Winter glut: farm prices of ₹2–5/kg; fruit dumped on roads.

signals: Arrivals and prices at Kolar and Madanapalle (Krishi Marata Vahini, Agmarknet).
IMD maximum temperatures in Kolar, Chittoor and Pune during Apr–Jun (fruit-set risk).
Whitefly and virus advisories from state horticulture departments.
Monsoon rainfall and landslide closures in Himachal (Solan–Delhi route) in Jul–Aug.
Area under nursery and transplanting reported by state agriculture departments.
business: Tomato is a weather-and-logistics business, not a storage business. Speed and sourcing from several belts at once is the edge.
Breaker-stage sourcing with controlled ripening (18–20 °C) cuts losses for quick commerce and QSR supply.
Processing (puree, paste) during the Jan–Mar glut is under-built; India still imports paste.
Price swings of 10x within six months are normal; contracts with price bands protect both farmer and buyer.
